title_en: Epigram on the Story of Clitophon and Leucippe
author: Photius of Constantinople (or Leo the Philosopher)
addressee: a friend (φίλος) who wishes to live chastely
occasion: A verse preface commending the novel of Achilles Tatius, Leucippe and Clitophon, to a reader who desires a chaste life; the epigram is transmitted under Photius's name, with a note that others attribute it to Leo the Philosopher.
argument: The epigram states that the story of Clitophon displays bitter love but a chaste life. It then presents Leucippe's supremely chaste life as amazing everyone, since she endured beating, shearing, abuse, and three deaths. The speaker urges the reader not to dwell on the incidental spectacle of the writing but to attend first to the movement of the story. The work, it says, escorts those who love wisely to the bridal chamber.

outline.move: The complete epigram is preserved here: it states that Clitophon's story displays bitter love but a chaste life, describes Leucippe's supremely chaste endurance, and urges the reader to attend to the story's movement rather than its incidental spectacle.
A fragmentary repetition of the opening, ending abruptly with the article ὁ before Λευκίππης.
A fragment preserving the middle portion about Leucippe's supremely chaste life and her endurance of beating, shearing, abuse, and three deaths.
A fragment preserving the closing portion, including the direct address to the reader as φίλος and the exhortation to attend to the story's movement.

scripture: No biblical citations or scriptural conventions are used in this epigram.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; the ninth century is inferred from the attributed authors.

The precise relationship of the epigram to the manuscript tradition of Achilles Tatius's novel is not established from the source alone.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The work, it says, escorts those who love wisely to the bridal chamber.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The work, it says, escorts those who desire/love wisely to the bridal chamber. Note: ποθοῦντας means 'those who desire/long for,' not specifically 'those who love wisely'—ἐμφρόνως ('sensibly/prudently') is the adverb modifying the escorting, not a description of the people themselves.

_unresolved_facts.claim: she endured beating, shearing, abuse, and three deaths
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: πῶς τετυμμένη κεκαρμένη τε καὶ κατηχρειωμένη, τὸ δὴ μέγιστον, τρὶς θανοῦσ' ἐκαρτέρει
_unresolved_facts.fix: she endured being struck, sheared, and treated with indignity/insulted—the greatest thing of all—having died three times. Note: The syntax shows τὸ δὴ μέγιστον ('the greatest thing of all') is a parenthetical intensifier referring to her endurance generally, not specifically to the three deaths; and the participles are passive (she was struck, sheared, insulted), not active.

_unresolved_facts.claim: A fragmentary repetition of the opening, ending abruptly with the article ὁ before Λευκίππης.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἔρωτα πικρόν, ἀλλὰ σώφρονα βίον ὁ Κλειτοφῶντος ὥσπερ ἐμφαίνει λόγος· ὁ
_unresolved_facts.fix: A fragmentary repetition of the opening, ending with the article ὁ before Λευκίππης (which begins the next clause in the complete text). Note: The article ὁ here belongs to ὁ Λευκίππης...βίος ('the life of Leucippe'), not 'before Λευκίππης' as if it were an isolated article; the fragment cuts off mid-sentence at the article that starts the next major clause.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The male protagonist of Achilles Tatius's novel; the genitive depends on λόγος, 'the story of Clitophon.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The male protagonist of Achilles Tatius's novel; the genitive Κλειτοφῶντος depends on λόγος, but ὁ...λόγος is the subject ('the story of Clitophon as it were displays/shows'). Note: The article ὁ goes with λόγος, not with Κλειτοφῶντος; the syntax is ὁ Κλειτοφῶντος...λόγος = 'the story of Clitophon' (with hyperbaton), not 'the Clitophon...story'.
